messages.name: Kun Wang
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: checking a sensory-to-action pathway
messages.body:
Dear Dr Wang,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I'm interested in neuroscience and decision-making, and chess gave me a question to explore: could a model using the adult fly connectome learn useful choices through experience?

Your work using functional imaging and single-neuron manipulation to trace sensory inputs toward descending neurons connects to a basic gap in my project. I have a board encoding and an output decoder, but that doesn't establish a biological path between them. Your earlier work on optic flow also made me think about how much information an input representation has to preserve. I understand that your fly work is larval. Which functional check would you require before assigning a sensory or action role to an annotated neuron class?

In six simple association tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three tests, so it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

I'd appreciate your honest view of whether this is a useful starting question. If you would consider occasional mentorship, I can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

messages.name: Pavithraa Seenivasan
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: what a neural readout says about a choice
messages.body:
Dear Dr Seenivasan,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. Chess and the public adult fly connectome led me to ask whether a model constrained by that wiring could learn useful decisions through experience and feedback.

Your work across the Jayaraman and Reiser labs connects to the sensory and action side of my project. I am trying to work out what evidence would link a neural readout to a choice, rather than just to a decoder I designed. I know that navigation and chess are different tasks. What neural or behavioral control would you use first to check whether an output reflects a circuit-supported choice?

In six simple association tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three tests, so it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you be open to occasional mentorship, starting with whether this part of the approach makes sense? I'd appreciate a candid assessment and can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: what a reduced memory model may leave out
messages.body:

Your research on dopamine-receptor splicing and your current interest in astrocytes and learning-induced plasticity connect to what my reduced model might be missing. messages.name: He Yang
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: what cell targeting can establish about learning
messages.body:
Dear Dr Yang,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a small circuit model could learn to make better decisions from puzzles and feedback.

Your contribution to the associative-learning driver-line resource connects to the neuron identities I still need to justify in my simulation. The resource pairs cell targeting with functional tests, which seems essential before treating a labeled population as a teaching pathway. I do not want to choose arbitrary cells and call the scalar I inject dopamine. What evidence would you require before using an identified population as the feedback target in a simplified model?

In six simple association tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three tests, so it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you be willing to offer a brief view on that question? If the project fits your interests, I'd also value occasional mentorship. I can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli

messages.name: Xianyuan Zhang
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: separating a motivational effect from stored learning
messages.body:
Dear Dr Zhang,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a small circuit model could learn to make better decisions from puzzles and feedback.

Your work on neuromodulatory circuits, especially the octopamine project described on your lab page, connects to how I should interpret feedback. I need to distinguish changing what a model wants or does immediately from changing what it remembers for later trials. I do not assume octopamine is an appropriate signal for chess feedback. What comparison would help separate a motivational effect from a stored association?

In six simple association tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three tests, so it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.
